title: When Networks Fail, Business Fails
summary: Friday, November 13th, 2026, brought a wave of outages for key services. Microsoft Outlook and the FAA experienced issues that halted email communications and grounded flights nationwide, leaving businesses, schools, and travelers stuck.
body_markdown:
Apparently, Friday the 13th decided to arrive early this year. Somewhere a black cat walked under a ladder, a bunch of people broke mirrors, and the technology gods decided to remind us just how interconnected and dependent the world has become on networks, cloud platforms, and digital infrastructure.


Between November 12 and 13, 2026, several major technology and infrastructure disruptions hit organizations and consumers around the world. Microsoft, the FAA, Workday, and Amtrak all made headlines due to the unfortunate coincidence that they all suffered significant network-related outages in the same time period, providing a good reason to take a hard look at how we currently monitor, manage, and protect our digital infrastructure.


## The Outages: What Happened, and What Was the Impact?


Here is a snapshot of the major disruptions:


- A widespread Microsoft 365 outage, lasting approximately 24 hours, disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and other services. Microsoft reported that “[a combination of a ‘latent defect,’ increased load, and lessened server capacity were among the cascading set of issues](https://x.com/clamanna/status/2122209697226948729?s=20) .” Tens of millions of employees across healthcare, manufacturing, financial services, government agencies, airlines, schools, and more, were affected. Financial impact to[Microsoft](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/cloud-observability) from productivity loss, subscription fee refunds, and actual economic loss[may reach $7 billion](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/12/business/live-news/microsoft-global-outage-intl-hnk?post-id=cmwf6e7el00003b6txhzlcvvg) , according to Anderson Economic Group.
- The payroll/human resources management company Workday’s outage of nearly 18 hours impacted more than 10,000 companies when part-time and full-time hourly employees were blocked from clocking into or out of their work shifts, checking schedules, or making schedule changes online at retail and restaurant companies. A problem involving a backup test of its disaster-recovery environment affected connections to production databases,[prompting Workday to restrict access to some production systems](https://www.newsweek.com/grounded-planes-dead-email-lost-satellites-technologys-very-bad-week-12718131) . This is expected to be an expensive outage, given Workday’s cloud[subscription revenue of approximately $27 million a day](https://fourweekmba.com/ai-workday-outage-backup-test-fault-hits-a-27m-a-day-service/) .
- The FAA outage resulting in a more-than four-hour nationwide ground stop brought U.S. airlines departures to a halt.[A single router in Arkansas that started a data overload](https://www.wsj.com/business/airlines/the-single-router-in-southern-arkansas-that-ground-air-travel-to-a-halt-eedc326c?st=cQc6qS&reflink=article_email_share) with excessive connection attempts overwhelmed parts of the FAA’s outdated network, causing travel interruptions for[approximately 1.5 million passengers](https://www.nerdwallet.com/travel/news/faa-ground-stop-refund) . More than 12,000 flights were cancelled or delayed, causing travelers to miss connections and activities. The financial impact on[airlines](https://www.netscout.com/industries/transportation/airlines) is already estimated for the four top U.S. carriers—American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines—to be[around $350 million](https://qz.com/airlines-345-million-faa-ground-stop-bernstein-111626) . Although the financial impact on individual passengers may never be accurately known, the human toll of missing family events and milestones such as weddings, athletic and arts performances, or birthdays and anniversaries will be remembered long after the credit cards are paid.
- Amtrak experienced a four-hour booking disruption due to the influx of traffic volume as travelers turned to the rail service as an alternative to air travel, stressing Amtrak’s booking system and customer support. Per[Amtrak’s publicly released financial disclosures](https://www.amtrak.com/content/dam/projects/dotcom/english/public/documents/corporate/financial/Amtrak-Management-Discussion-Analysis-Audited-Financial-Statements-FY2025.pdf) , average daily ticket revenue is $7.4 million. The nationwide aviation ground stop represented a major revenue windfall for[rail services](https://www.netscout.com/industries/transportation/train-rail) that was largely missed due to the booking outage. Cost increases associated with customer service overtime will add to Amtrak’s financial impact.


Although these incidents had differing causes, they all demonstrate how rapidly disruptions can affect interconnected businesses and essential services.


## The Problem Is What We Aren’t Seeing in Our Networks


Corporate network investments vary from modernizing legacy technologies in some environments to investing in AI transformations in others. The speed and variety of technology introductions may leave gaps in coverage. It means organizations need to rethink their strategy to move from reactive approaches with traditional monitoring tools to more proactive, predictive, and preventive approaches leveraging packet-derived intelligence from end-to-end[network observability](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/network-observability) solutions.


Modernization is not a single destination. Rather, it’s a journey that involves cloud,[hybrid](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/cloud-observability) , on-premises, legacy, and emerging technologies, all of which must work together. Regardless of where an organization is on this journey, it is worth repeating that you can’t manage what you can’t see.


AI can be a powerful accelerator in this evolution, but it is only as effective as the data feeding it. Incomplete visibility, disconnected monitoring tools, and poor-quality telemetry produce incomplete insights and possibly misinformed decisions. And more telemetry does not automatically create better decision-making; only relevant context and supporting evidence can.


## Transformation and Modernization Starts with Observability


Packet-derived intelligence independently observes applications, services, transactions, networks, and user interactions end-to-end. Early semantic extraction preserves operational meaning at the point of observation. High-fidelity, packet-derived, AI-ready[Smart Data](https://www.netscout.com/what-is/smart-data) from NETSCOUT provides a common, evidence-based view of what is actually happening across an organization’s network. As IT teams avoid relying on incomplete telemetry or conflicting vendor tool assessments, they confidently pinpoint root causes, collaborate with technology partners, and accelerate service restoration. This shared source of truth is essential where a single service disruption can affect multiple systems, locations, operational partners, and customers simultaneously.


You need the right data, comprehensive observability, and intelligent analysis across the entire digital ecosystem, not just the newest or most modern areas. Friday the 13th, 2026, may have provided the punch line, but the outages provided a critical lesson. The question is not whether another outage will happen. It’s whether your organization will see the warning signs to predict and prevent the chaos we have just seen.


The ultimate goal of observability isn’t about becoming better at explaining why everything went down. It is about using AI-ready Smart Data to proactively provide insights to predict issues ahead of time and empowering your organization to take necessary steps to minimize impact, or even better, prevent an outage.
